findings.title: Fires around acquiring or documenting discrete information and images—photos, screenshots, survey data, contact details, or records—though some activations appear incidental.
Fires around recording or filming ongoing audiovisual events, especially cameras rolling, people being filmed, and recorded performances.
Fires at sentence or section transitions, especially the first word after punctuation or a line break, often introducing explanatory prose or a new heading.
Fires on webpage scaffolding and fragments—headings, list labels, legal boilerplate, attribution tags, and procedural or headline text—rather than continuous prose.
Mostly technical and scientific publication text—especially citations and author affiliations—with a security-vulnerability notice as a related technical-document outlier.
The snippets span unrelated web content and document types; the firing points are varied formatting or ordinary words rather than a coherent semantic pattern.
Fires on specialized, technical, or structured web text—device specs, software instructions, domain terminology, measurements, lists, and wiki markup—rather than one narrow subject.
Fires on ordinary editorial and consumer-facing prose, including news, lifestyle, and promotional articles, with no clear shared topic beyond that general writing style.
Fires on short grammatical linking words, including an infinitival “to” and a preposition in the phrase “out of place.”
The marked spans range from punctuation and whitespace to ordinary words, numbers, and word fragments, with no clear shared pattern.
Often fires at a direct reply or answer in forum and support exchanges, including nearby punctuation; the marked words themselves vary widely.
Fires on hesitation and thinking-aloud cues in informal answers—fillers like “hmm” and “huh,” ellipses, and phrases like “let’s see.”
Fires on academic bibliography publisher names, especially Elsevier, Springer, and Taylor & Francis, within citation-heavy scholarly text.
Mostly fires on party-role labels in legal case captions, such as Defendant, Plaintiff, and Respondent, but the film metadata and other examples do not fit that pattern.
Fires mainly on punctuation and formatting boundaries—sentence or section endings, delimiters, and line breaks—in structured web text.
No stable negative pattern is evident: marked positions range from ellipses and brackets to ordinary words and sentence breaks in unrelated text.
Marks points where prose pivots into an added clarification, resource, list, or named item—often a connective or punctuation, or the first word of the supplement.
No stable shared role is apparent: marked items range from technical digits and hardware or space terms to ordinary verbs, pronouns, and blog language.
Marks quantities, counts, and plural collections, especially when describing many items, complete sets, or totals.
Marks grouped or selectable alternatives—such as both options, a choice of several items, or a range of times or values.
The pole fires strongly on “once” as a temporal or conditional connective, marking what happens after an event or prerequisite.
Many firings mark words at the end of temporal or conditional clauses, often naming a state or threshold reached, though a few examples are unrelated.
Fires in structured informational web copy—headlines, listings, and short descriptions of places, products, services, or organizations—often around details or transitions.
The examples span ads, SEO text, reviews, tutorials, and articles, with no clear shared feature beyond being web content.
Tracks visual attention and eye contact—looking, scanning faces, and reading emotion or connection through someone’s eyes.
Often marks spoken interpersonal exchange, including chatter, telling, talking, and murmuring; some firings land on adjacent actions or incidental words.
Favors sentence or discourse transitions—new statements and clauses, often marked by sentence-final punctuation or an opening word—rather than one particular topic.
Favors words and punctuation continuing ordinary syntax within a sentence, especially function words and list separators; a few formatting and heading examples are exceptions.
The marked fragments occur in unrelated words and contexts, with no consistent semantic or grammatical pattern apparent.
Fires on references to humans and the human world, often framed from a cat, fairy, or alien perspective as an outside group.
Marks open-ended choices or generalization—“whatever,” “any,” and “no matter what”—often in advice about selecting among options or pursuing a goal.
Often marks fragments of Indian or other geographic and personal names, with occasional nearby punctuation, whitespace, or ordinary words suggesting noisy tokenization.
Favors structured commercial web copy—product specifications, bullet labels, and property listings—rather than one particular subject; the marked tokens often sit at labels or item boundaries.
No stable shared feature is evident: firings range from whitespace and word fragments to ordinary words across unrelated prose and listings.
Firings span unrelated topics and include arbitrary word fragments, ordinary words, numbers, and punctuation; no consistent semantic or formatting pattern is evident.
Firings likewise mix unrelated content, function words, names, numbers, and punctuation, without a stable shared pattern beyond occurring in web text.
Fires mainly on punctuation and delimiters that close or separate units, especially code punctuation and commas at clause or byline boundaries.
Often marks words for people, occupations, or social roles (such as administrator, coordinator, spokesperson, wife, and son), but several examples are unrelated technical or organizational nouns.
Favors promotional business copy and customer endorsements presenting services, products, or providers positively, across varied local-business categories.
Favors procedural or troubleshooting material that explains how to repair, configure, install, or otherwise handle a practical or technical issue.
Marks numeric limits and bounds, especially phrases such as “up to,” “as low as,” and “less than or equal to,” with some incidental numeric-field tokens.
Marks technical measurement and specification terminology—such as temperature, range, focal length, voltage, and frequency response—often in product or scientific data.
Favors informal blog-like prose, especially personal anecdotes and practical household or cooking instructions, rather than a consistent word meaning.
The examples span factual reporting, reviews, reference-style descriptions, and personal narratives, with no reliable shared pattern beyond general web prose.
Mostly fires on “it/its” as anaphoric pronouns or possessives, with a few related deictic or referential forms such as “this,” “there,” and “then.”

Fires on relational and connective terms expressing cause or result (“therefore,” “consequence,” “resulting”), as well as spatial or temporal relations (“between,” “underneath,” “afterward,” “follow”).
The marked tokens span unrelated grammatical roles and topics, with no consistent contextual pattern beyond ordinary web-text words and punctuation.
These examples likewise mix unrelated topics and common function words, without a stable shared linguistic or semantic pattern.
Often marks capitalized name or title material, including subword fragments, though the number and “himself” are notable outliers.
Commas and spacing tokens recur, but other firings mark unrelated word fragments and ordinary words, with no clear shared pattern.
Firings are scattered across topics, but often land on connective words in neutral, explanatory or reference-style prose; no more specific shared content pattern is clear.
Firings strongly cluster around “God” and spiritual or religious reflection, with a few month-name and other stray examples that do not form a clear second pattern.
The marked items span unrelated parts of speech and contexts, with no consistent semantic or grammatical pattern apparent.
The examples are similarly heterogeneous; a few marks fall inside names or hyphenated words, but this does not explain the rest.
Fires on general principles or guiding standards proposed to shape policy, design, or practice across varied domains.
The examples are scattered, with no reliable shared pattern; several involve religious or scholarly texts, but many do not.
Often occurs in contexts of hoping, waiting, or searching for a desired or anticipated outcome, though several firings are incidental.
The firings span unrelated topics and mostly land on ordinary function words or punctuation, with no stable shared pattern.
Often marks language that characterizes or evaluates something—its traits, significance, reputation, or standout quality—with occasional function words inside those descriptions.
No clear shared semantic job: the marks span grammatical connectors and punctuation in unrelated prayer, quiz, informational, advertising, and job-description text.
Firings span unrelated prose, tables, and corrupted text, often on ordinary function words or arbitrary word fragments, with no consistent semantic or structural pattern.
Fires on trivia and test material—especially crossword clue archives and quiz questions that prompt recall of names, events, or facts.
The pole includes age suffixes and numeric or mathematical notation, but also unrelated punctuation, names, and ordinary words; no single pattern explains the examples.
Most hits are common grammatical or connective words in ordinary prose, though a few content-word fragments and technical terms are exceptions.
